During the 10th to 12th centuries the territory of the present-day oblast was part of Kievan Rusʹ. From the 13th through the 18th centuries most of these lands came under Tatar rule,except for the South-West Prychornomori︠a︡ Region which was seized by the Lytovsʹke Velyke Kni︠a︡zivstvo [Lithuania (Grand Duchy)]. Throughout the 17th to 18th centuries much of the territory of today's Odesʹka oblastʹ was subjected to raids bythe Bilhorodsʹka and I︠E︡dysansʹka hordes which themselves were subordinated to the Crimean Khanate [Krymskoe khanstvo]. After the Russian-Turkish War of 1787-1791 these lands were formally ceded to Russia, and they became part of theNovorosiĭsʹka hubernii︠a︡ [no publs. in LC data base] from 1797 to 1802, then were transferred to the Khersonsʹka hubernii︠a︡ from 1803 onwards On Jan. 30, 1918 Soviet rule was established in Odesa, however during the same year the BessarabiaRegion was seized by Romania while the Odesa Region was invaded by Austro-Hungarian forces. Throughout 1919 these regions were occupied by Interventionist and then White Army forces. By Feb. 1920 the Odesa Region itself had been liberated bySoviet forces and the Odesʹka hubernii︠a︡ was established. In Nov. 1922 the Mykolaïvsʹka hubernii︠a︡ merged with the Odesʹka hubernii︠a︡. During the jurisdictional reorganization of 1925 the Odesʹka hubernii︠a︡ was abolished and the Odesʹkyĭokruh [ Odesk̇a okruha] [no publs. in LC data base] was formed. On 27 Feb. 1932 the Odesk̇a oblast ̇was established. During 1937 the Mykolaèivsk̇a oblast ̇was separated from the Odesk̇a oblast,̇ and in 1939 ten rayons of the Odesk̇a oblastẇere transferred to the Kirovohradsk̇a oblast.̇ In 1940 eight rayons of the former Moldavsk̇a ARSR were given to the Odesk̇a oblast.̇ Finally, in 1954 the territory of the former Izmaèilṡk̇a oblast</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">Nat. Ukraïny:</subfield><subfield code="b">v. 2, p. 52-56 (Lʹvivsʹka oblastʹ; established 12-04-1939. During the 10th to 12th centuries this territory belonged to Kievan Rusʹ. From the middle of the 12th cent. it was part of the Halyt︠s︡ʹke then Volodymyro-Volynsʹke kni︠a︡zivstvo. In1241 this area was invaded by Mongol-Tatar forces. From 1340 to 1387 these Halychyna lands were fought over by Poles and Hungarians, with Poland emerging as the conqueror. From the middle of the 15th cent. the territory of present-day Lʹvivsʹkaoblastʹ had become part of the Rusʹke [Ruskie województwo] and Belzʹke voi︠e︡vodstvo [Bełskie województwo] [no publs. in LC data base], where it remained until the first partition of Poland in 1772. From 1772 the Halychyna lands then became partof Austria (later the Austro-Hungarian Empire) until Nov. 1918 when this empire collapsed. By July 1919 the East Halychyna lands were at first seized by Poland, then liberated in July 1920 by the Red Army which established the Halyt︠s︡ʹkaSot︠s︡ialistychna Radi︠a︡nsʹka Respublika [no publs. in LC data base]). However by autumn of 1920 the East Halychyna lands were reoccupied by Poland and became part of the Lʹvivsʹke voi︠e︡vodstvo (Lwowskie Województwo). In Sept. 1939 the RedArmy liberated all the territory of the Halychyna lands and on Oct. 1, 1939 declared the reunification of West Ukraine with Soviet Ukraine. In 1959 the territory of the Drohobyt︠s︡ʹka oblastʹ [no publs. in LC data base] was added to the Lʹvivsk̇a oblast,̇ and in 1961 six villages from the Volynsk̇a oblast ̇were also added)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">SSSR, admin.-territ. otdelenie, 1977:</subfield><subfield code="b">p. 309 (Lʹvovskai︠a︡ oblastʹ; established 12-04-1939; capitol city is Lʹvov)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">Ukr. rad. ent︠s︡ykl.:</subfield><subfield code="b">v. 2, p. 310 (Lʹvivsʹka oblastʹ)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">BGN gaz., USSR:</subfield><subfield code="b">v. 5 (Lʹvovskaya oblastʹ; OBLT. 50p0s 00ʹ N., 24p0s 00ʹ E.)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="675" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">Lustracja Województwa ruskiego, 1661-1665, 1970-1976: t.p. It was established in 1932)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">Encyc. of Ukraine:</subfield><subfield code="b">v. 2 (articles under Kharkiv, Kharkiv gubernia, Kharkiv oblast, and Kharkiv Regiment: the Kharkiv raion [Xarkiv raion] is part of the territory that was once constituted Slobidska Ukraine. In the 17th and 18th centuries itconstituted parts of the Kharkiv and Izium Regiments. Later these lands became part of the Slobidska Ukraine gubernia [Slobidsʹka-Ukraïnsʹka hubernii︠a︡] (1765-80, 1796-1835), then part of the Kharkiv Vicegerency [Kharkivsʹke namisnyt︠s︡tvo](1780-1796), then of Kharkiv gubernia [Kharʹkovskai︠a︡ gubernii︠a︡ ] (1835-1925). The Kharkiv gubernia consisted of 11 counties, one of which was the Kharkiv county [Kharkivsʹkyĭ povit]. Under Soviet rule the gubernia was abolished in 1925 andreplaced by the Kharkiv, Izium, Kupianka, and Sumy okruhas. In 1932 these okruhas were replaced by the Kharkiv oblast)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="670" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">SSSR, admin.-territ. delenie, 1983:</subfield><subfield code="b">p. 328 (under Kharʹkovskai︠a︡ oblastʹ: Kharʹkovskiĭ raĭon)</subfield></datafield><datafield tag="675" ind1=" " ind2=" "><subfield code="a">LC data base, 09-18-96 (hdg.: Kharkivsʹka okruha (Ukraine) )</subfield></datafield></record>
